content:
People can usually tell when an AI headshot is bad. They cannot usually tell when it is AI. The two are not the same thing, and mixing them up is why so many people either avoid AI headshots entirely or upload one with plastic skin and hope nobody looks closely.

Every tell that gives an AI headshot away has a specific cause, and most of those causes sit in the photos you upload rather than in the model. This guide lists the tells, explains where each one comes from, and then covers what viewers actually judge in the first instant, which has nothing to do with how the file was made.

Can people tell a headshot is AI generated?

Only when something is wrong with it. A viewer looking at a profile photo is not running a provenance check, they are reading a face. If the skin has texture, the light on the face matches the light in the room, and the expression is one you actually make, the photo passes the same way a good photograph passes.

If the skin is poreless, the face is a generic average, or the background is lit from a different direction than the face, the photo fails, and the viewer files it under "fake" without knowing or caring which tool produced it.

At a glance: the tells and what causes them

The tellWhat people seeThe usual cause
Plastic skinNo pores, no fine lines, a waxy sheenOver-smoothing, or too few sharp photos for the model to learn real texture
Nobody in particularA pleasant face that is not quite youToo few photos, or photos that all look the same, so the model averages toward a generic face
Mismatched lightFace lit from the left, room lit from the rightA swapped or pasted face rather than a whole image generated around your face
Odd detailsHands, ears, teeth or glasses that are slightly wrongSmall, complex structures the model saw too rarely in the input
An expression you never makeFriends say "that is not your smile"Input photos with one forced expression, or none at all
Two of youSet looks like several different peopleWithin-person variability in the input was too wide, or the input was too narrow to anchor the face

Why does AI headshot skin look plastic?

Poreless skin is the tell most people name first, and it has two causes that often show up together. The first is over-smoothing: some tools apply a beauty pass that flattens texture, and the result looks like a mannequin under studio light. The second is thin input.

A model can only reproduce texture it has seen, so if your photos are soft, small, compressed or shot in dim light, there is no texture to learn and the model fills the gap with a smooth guess.

The fix is at the upload stage. Sharp, well-lit photos where you can see pores and the odd freckle give the model real skin to work with. Picturesk asks for 5 to 15 recent selfies, with 10 to 12 as the sweet spot, and screens every photo before you pay so that a blurry or too-small face is flagged rather than quietly ruining the set.

Why does an AI headshot look like nobody in particular?

This is the subtler tell, and it is the one that makes colleagues pause without being able to say why. The face is symmetrical, pleasant and completely forgettable. It happens when the model does not have enough information to pin down what makes your face yours, so it drifts toward an average.

The research on faces explains why input variety matters so much. Jenkins, White, Van Montfort and Burton showed in Cognition (2011) that different photos of the same unfamiliar face vary so much that people often sort them into piles as if they were different people. A single photo is not a reliable record of a face, and within-person variability can be larger than the difference between two people.

For an AI headshot that cuts both ways. Ten near-identical selfies from one angle in one light tell the model almost nothing beyond that one view, so it invents the rest. Ten photos across different days, angles, lighting and expressions show the model what stays constant when everything else changes, and that constant is you.

Why does the light on the face not match the background?

When the face is lit warmly from the left and the office behind it is lit coolly from the right, the eye notices before the brain does. This is the signature of a swapped face: a single reference photo pasted or conditioned onto a stock body in a stock scene. The face and the scene were never in the same room, and it shows in the shadows under the jaw and the highlights on the forehead.

A model trained on your face works differently, because the whole image is generated around you, so the light on your face is the light in the scene. That is the method Picturesk uses: we train a model on your face from your photos, then generate the set across the backgrounds and outfits you chose. It is slower and costs more to run than a swap, which is why the result is delivered by email in about an hour rather than in seconds.

What about hands, ears, teeth and glasses?

Small, intricate structures are where generated images most often slip. Hands have too many joints, ears have folds that vary from person to person, teeth have a specific count and spacing, and glasses have frames that must sit on the nose and reflect the light in a plausible way. If the model saw these rarely in your input, it improvises, and improvised ears are wrong in a way people cannot name but do notice.

Practical steps that help:

  • If you wear glasses daily, wear them in most of your photos, and keep the lenses free of heavy reflections.
  • Include a couple of open-mouth smiles if that is how you smile, so the model has seen your teeth.
  • Keep hair off your ears in at least a few shots.
  • Do not worry about hands: a headshot crop should end at the shoulders, and if a generated image shows hands, pick a different one from the set.

Why is the expression wrong?

An expression you never make is the tell that fools strangers and catches everyone who knows you. The cause is almost always the input.

If every uploaded selfie has the same tight, camera-facing half-smile, the model learns that one expression and stretches it across the set. If the input has no smiles at all, the model borrows a smile from its general training, and that smile belongs to someone else.

Give it a range: a relaxed neutral face, a small closed-mouth smile, a proper laugh, something in between. The expression that ends up in your chosen headshot should be one your friends have actually seen on you.

What do people actually judge in the first instant?

Here is the other half of the answer, and it matters more than the tells. Willis and Todorov found that people form judgments of trustworthiness, competence, likeability and attractiveness from a face after about 100 milliseconds of exposure, and that looking longer mostly makes them more confident rather than changing their mind, as Princeton reported when the study was published. Nobody spends 100 milliseconds asking how a file was made.

Todorov and colleagues later showed in PNAS (2008) that face evaluation is organised around two dimensions, trustworthiness and dominance, and that features resembling a positive expression push trustworthiness up. That is the test your headshot is really sitting: does this face look like someone I would trust and hire? A good AI headshot passes it the way a good photograph does, because the viewer is responding to a face, not to a technology.

It also means the same person can score very differently across photos. Vernon, Sutherland, Young and Hartley found in PNAS (2014) that first impressions vary substantially across different images of one person, driven by lighting, pose and expression. Which is a useful reframe: the goal is not to hide that a photo is AI, it is to get the lighting, pose and expression right, whoever pressed the shutter.

How do you check your own AI headshots before using one?

Two checks, both quick. First, put the generated headshot next to a real, recent, unedited photo of yourself on the same screen and look at the skin, the eyes, the shape of the nose and the line of the jaw. If your eye keeps snagging on one feature, that feature is the tell, and you should pick a different image from the set or go back and fix the input.

Second, ask two or three people who see you regularly, and ask them a specific question: "Does this look like me on a normal day?" Do not ask "Is this AI?", because it primes them to hunt for flaws. People who know you are the harshest test, because they carry a stable memory of your face that a stranger does not. If they hesitate, listen to what they hesitate about.

If the answer is no, the fix is nearly always more and better photos, not a different tool. That is also why Picturesk carries a look-like-you guarantee: if the set does not look like you, reply to the delivery email within 3 days and you get a full refund, and you keep the images either way.

Is it honest to use an AI headshot?

The rule that matters most is LinkedIn's own. Its profile photo guidelines say the photo must reflect your likeness, and LinkedIn may remove photos that consist solely of someone else's likeness, stock imagery, celebrities, logos or the like. The guidelines are about whether the photo is you, not about whether a camera or a model produced it.

So the honesty line is simple: the photo must look like you in person. If a recruiter would recognise you from it in the lobby, it is honest. If it shows a version of you that is ten years younger, thirty pounds lighter, with different teeth and someone else's smile, it is not, and it will cost you the trust it was supposed to buy.

A properly made set from an AI headshot generator should clear that bar comfortably, because the whole point of training a model on your face is that the result is your face.

faqs.question: Can recruiters tell if a headshot is AI generated?
faqs.answer: Only if it is a poor one. Recruiters read the face, not the file, and research shows people judge trustworthiness and competence within about 100 milliseconds. A headshot with real skin texture, consistent lighting and your own expression passes like a photograph, while plastic skin or a generic face is what gets noticed.

faqs.question: What are the most common signs of an AI headshot?
faqs.answer: Poreless, waxy skin; a face that is pleasant but not quite anyone; light on the face that disagrees with the background; odd ears, teeth or glasses; and an expression the person never makes. Each has a cause, and most come from too few, too similar or too soft input photos.

faqs.question: Why does my AI headshot not look like me?
faqs.answer: Almost always because the input was thin. Too few photos, or photos that all share one angle, one light and one expression, give the model nothing to anchor your face, so it drifts toward an average. Upload 10 to 12 sharp, recent selfies across different days, angles and expressions.

faqs.question: Is it against LinkedIn rules to use an AI headshot?
faqs.answer: No. LinkedIn's profile photo guidelines require the photo to reflect your likeness and prohibit stock images, celebrities, logos and other people, but they do not ban AI generated images. The practical test is whether someone would recognise you in person from the photo, and if so it meets the rule.

faqs.question: How do I check whether my AI headshot looks real?
faqs.answer: Put it next to a recent, unedited photo of yourself and compare skin, eyes, nose and jaw. Then ask two or three people who see you often whether it looks like you on a normal day, without mentioning AI. If they hesitate, choose another image from the set or improve your input photos.
